overview: The Maratha state founded by Shivaji in the Western Ghats broke Mughal power in the eighteenth century and, as a confederacy of chiefs under the Peshwa at Pune, ruled or taxed most of India by the 1750s. Its horsemen, hill forts and revenue administration made it the last great Indian power before the British.

items.text: Light cavalry that lived off the country and struck and withdrew defeated slower Mughal armies.
Shivaji's chain of hill forts, Raigad, Pratapgad and Sinhagad among them, controlled the passes of the Western Ghats.
A navy under Kanhoji Angre held the Konkan coast against the Portuguese, the Siddis and the East India Company.
Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in a Vedic ceremony asserting independent Hindu kingship.
The Ashtapradhan, a council of eight ministers, ran war, revenue, foreign affairs and religion.
Marathi, with Sanskrit terms replacing Persian ones in Shivaji's chancery, became the language of state.
Revenue came as chauth and sardeshmukhi, a quarter and a tenth of the yield, collected directly from the land.
The Maratha wars drained the Mughals; after the defeat at Panipat in 1761 the confederacy recovered and held Delhi's emperor as a client.
Marathi identity and the memory of Shivaji remain central in Maharashtra.

fall.text: The East India Company beat the confederacy in three wars; the Peshwa surrendered in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War and his lands were annexed.
